title: COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya  - Carbon Brief
gist: COP31 in Antalya ended as the longest COP ever with the presidency's 'Antalya pact' rejected by the EU, UK and climate-vulnerable states for omitting fossil fuels and adaptation-finance figures, amid a 70% drop in climate-finance pledges. Outside the negotiations, ~80 countries backed a 35%-electricity-by-2035 target and coalitions advancing fossil-fuel exit roadmaps grew, while producer states blocked mitigation and fossil-fuel language.

themes.theme: COP31 outcome: rejected 'Antalya pact' and longest COP ever

insights.claim: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, failed to adopt its presidency-led 'Antalya pact' cover decision, which was rejected by at least 32 countries including the EU, UK and several climate-vulnerable nations because it lacked clear references to fossil fuels and climate finance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals the UN consensus process cannot currently deliver new top-down fossil-fuel or finance commitments; policy momentum shifts to coalitions and national action.
insights.quote: The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 counties
insights.locator: Cover decision

insights.claim: COP31's final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time, nearly 50 hours after the scheduled end, making it the longest COP in history.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Illustrates escalating dysfunction of the multilateral climate process, which raises policy uncertainty for climate-linked investment.
insights.quote: nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end
insights.locator: Turkish and Australian leadership

insights.claim: Experts argue the rejection of the COP31 cover decision was not a 'collapse' like Copenhagen, but the first time high-ambition countries actively rejected a lowest-common-denominator text, as several negotiated items were still adopted.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reframes the failure as a shift in high-ambition bloc tactics rather than a breakdown, implying future COPs may see more walk-aways rather than weak compromises.
insights.quote: those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer
insights.locator: Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly

insights.claim: A 126-country coalition spanning the EU, UK, AOSIS, AILAC, the Umbrella Group, EIG and the LDCs approached the COP31 presidency as a united front demanding changes on fossil-fuel transition language, adaptation finance and carbon capture, with one observer calling EU–AOSIS cooperation of this closeness 'unprecedented'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A large, cross-north-south pro-phaseout bloc is consolidating, which raises the long-run probability of coordinated fossil-fuel transition policy outside consensus channels.
insights.locator: Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries

insights.claim: Failure of the COP31 cover decision may end the recent trend of COPs attempting cover decisions and spark renewed efforts to reform the UN climate process; French ex-chief negotiator Paul Watkinson said there are limits to political signals in a decision.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Future COPs may produce fewer headline political statements, reducing their signalling value for markets.
insights.quote: there are limits to political signals in a decision
insights.locator: Paul Watkinson, the French chief negotiator

insights.claim: Observers said more than double the negotiating time in COP31's first week went to the presidency's cover decision than to mandated items such as the global goal on adaptation, the mitigation work programme and the just transition work programme, crowding out technical work.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shows how presidency-driven political deals can starve technical implementation workstreams, slowing rules that govern finance and markets.
insights.locator: Observers told Carbon Brief that there

insights.claim: Calls for COP reform intensified after COP31: UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell said there is scope to 'improve, modernise and reform', Peru for AILAC called for a clear rule on votes and an independent efficiency review, and Panama's minister called the COP 'an exercise in futility'; formal discussion continues under the AIM agenda in Bonn in 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A possible move away from strict consensus (e.g. voting rules) would materially change the odds of binding fossil-fuel outcomes.
insights.quote: The COP has become an exercise in futility
insights.locator: COP reform was discussed during the summit

themes.theme: Fossil fuels: consensus blocked, coalitions of the willing grow

insights.claim: All later drafts of the COP31 cover decision omitted any direct mention of fossil fuels; the final version only 'recalled' the COP28 UAE consensus 'in its entirety', which Joanna Depledge called 'near meaningless'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The consensus-based transition-away-from-fossil-fuels signal stalled at the COP28 level, reducing near-term multilateral pressure on oil and gas demand.
insights.locator: This one also did not directly mention fossil fuels

insights.claim: Russia steadfastly opposed any wording on fossil fuels at COP31, arguing there is an ongoing role for oil and gas even in 1.5C pathways, while Saudi Arabia for the Arab group objected to labelling CCUS as greenwashing.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Producer-state veto power remains decisive in UN talks, protecting oil and gas from multilateral phase-down language.
insights.locator: Russia explained its steadfast opposition

insights.claim: The COP31 second-draft cover text included numerical carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) targets, apparently as a 'quid pro quo' for the quantified 35%-by-2035 electrification target; the 126-country coalition asked for them to be deleted, but the final draft merely softened 'accelerating' to 'increasing'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: CCUS is being traded as a political concession to producers, a signal of its role as fossil-fuel incumbents' preferred transition pathway.
insights.quote: apparently as “quid pro quo” for the quantified electrification target
insights.locator: Controversially, this menu of options

insights.claim: Eight European and small island nations announced national roadmaps away from fossil fuels at COP31 (including Denmark, Spain, Portugal, Luxembourg and Vanuatu, plus a Pacific regional roadmap), bringing the total with such plans to 27.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: National fossil-fuel exit roadmaps are proliferating outside consensus, creating country-specific demand-decline policy risk.
insights.locator: In addition, eight European and small island nations

insights.claim: A second transitioning-away-from-fossil-fuels conference, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland, will hold a pre-conference in Dublin in May 2027 and the main conference in Tuvalu in July 2027, with a third planned for 2028; the first, in Santa Marta in April 2026, drew 57 countries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Parallel fossil-fuel transition forums are institutionalising, giving dates to watch for coordinated policy announcements.
insights.locator: They confirmed that a pre-conference

insights.claim: Colombia's former environment minister Irene Vélez Torres said countries committed to transitioning away from fossil fuels will act regardless of consensus, declaring that consensus 'is not going to stop us anymore'.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Climate policy is shifting to 'two-tier multilateralism' where willing coalitions move ahead, fragmenting regulatory landscapes across countries.
insights.quote: Consensus as a method is not going to stop us anymore
insights.locator: She told the huddle that, regardless

insights.claim: China's climate envoy Liu Zhenmin said 'phasing out fossil fuels' is a proposition of a small number of countries that has never constituted consensus and that the transition requires gradually replacing fossil fuels over decades.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The world's largest emitter openly rejects phase-out framing, supporting a long tail of fossil-fuel demand.
insights.quote: is merely a proposition of a small number of countries and has never constituted a consensus
insights.locator: “‘Phasing out fossil fuels’

insights.claim: During COP31, the presidents of China, the US and Russia declared at the APEC Summit that they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products in response to global energy shocks.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Major powers are prioritising energy security and supply expansion over climate pledges, bullish for refining and oil-product supply chains.
insights.quote: plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products
insights.locator: A few days later and thousands of miles away

themes.theme: Electrification as the new organising theme

insights.claim: Around 80 nations signed up to a voluntary COP31 target to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 ('35 by 35'), though a full list of signatories was never published.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A broad, IRENA-aligned electrification target supports structural demand for grids, renewables, heat pumps, EVs and power equipment.
insights.locator: COP31 president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary

insights.claim: The COP31 presidency framed electrification as a practical route to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with Australia's Chris Bowen saying 'There’s no better way than electrification', while critics saw it as a substitute for dropping explicit fossil-fuel language.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Electrification is becoming the politically palatable framing for decarbonisation, even among producer-sensitive governments.
insights.quote: There’s no better way than electrification
insights.locator: “The world agreed at COP28

insights.claim: The COP31 'electrification delivery package' included 14 initiatives, among them a maritime goal of 20% electricity share of shipping's final energy demand by 2035 and the Electrify Now Finance Coalition aiming to mobilise over $1.2bn for clean electrification in developing countries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Points to emerging capital pools and targets for shipping electrification, grid investment and emerging-market clean power.
insights.locator: Towards the end of COP31, the presidency

insights.claim: The Global Renewables Alliance said at least 25 nations have put in place electrification policies since the start of the 'Hormuz crisis', framing renewables plus electrification as the formula for secure, affordable energy.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Energy-security shocks are accelerating electrification policy, a structural tailwind for renewables and electrified end-uses.
insights.quote: renewable energy plus electrification equals secure, affordable and clean energy for all consumers
insights.locator: At a coalition launch event

insights.claim: China and Australia issued a joint statement backing electrification on a voluntary basis and mentioning the 35-by-35 goal, but it did not mention fossil fuels and warned climate measures should not be a disguised restriction on international trade; one academic said it mostly confirms existing unambitious positions.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China supports electrification (where it dominates manufacturing) while resisting fossil phase-out and trade barriers on cleantech.
insights.locator: In it, the two countries

insights.claim: China signed an agreement with Turkey to invest $15bn in developing 7GW of solar and wind and 4GW of transmission capacity, which analysts frame as China exercising influence through real-economy deals rather than formal climate-finance accounting.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Chinese state-backed capital is a growing driver of renewable and grid build-out in emerging markets.
insights.locator: China also signed an agreement with Turkey

themes.theme: Climate finance retreat and adaptation/loss-and-damage gaps

insights.claim: Public climate-finance pledges have dropped 70% amid developed-country aid cuts, and pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years with few new commitments at COP31; Australia, Germany, France and Japan were criticised for not committing new funds.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shrinking public concessional finance raises the cost of capital for emerging-market clean energy and adaptation projects.
insights.quote: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.
insights.locator: Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts

insights.claim: Roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries, and this provision now looks less certain amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Defence spending is crowding out climate aid, shifting the burden toward MDBs and private capital under the $300bn NCQG.
insights.locator: In recent years, roughly a third

insights.claim: EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said 'any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water', and developed countries insisted finance talks be based on the existing $300bn-by-2035 mobilisation goal while pushing to broaden the contributor base to wealthier developing countries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Developed-country fiscal ceilings on climate aid are hardening; expect pressure on China and Gulf states to contribute.
insights.quote: any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water
insights.locator: Prior to COP31, Wopke Hoekstra

insights.claim: COP31 failed to give any baseline or figure for tripling adaptation finance; developing countries wanted $120bn by 2035 on a 2025 baseline, France reportedly proposed a 2019 baseline implying just $60bn, while UNEP estimates developing countries need $305bn a year by 2035.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A large and growing adaptation funding gap signals underinvestment in resilience infrastructure and rising physical-risk exposure in emerging markets.
insights.locator: NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported

insights.claim: The climate finance work programme outcome at COP31 was largely procedural, with tripling adaptation finance, burden-sharing and donor-base expansion stripped out, but talks will continue until 2028 rather than ending next year as some developed countries wanted.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No new binding finance obligations emerged; the issue stays live through 2028.
insights.locator: This was reflected in the final decisions

insights.claim: COP31 resolved the adaptation fund's board composition using 'developed'/'developing' language, enabling the fund to receive 5% of proceeds from the Article 6.4 Paris carbon market, a revenue stream insulated from national budget politics.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Creates a structural link between carbon-credit market volumes and adaptation funding.
insights.quote: which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes
insights.locator: Thwaites described the resolution

insights.claim: The UN fund for loss and damage has received just $342m in pledges against $2.8bn in funding requests, will not start disbursing until December, and new pledges at COP31 were limited to €15m from Spain plus formalised Italian and EU pledges; its first replenishment starts in 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Climate-disaster compensation remains drastically underfunded, leaving vulnerable economies to absorb losses.
insights.locator: So far, predominantly developed nations

insights.claim: Brazil's Tropical Forest Forever Facility has mobilised $8.2bn, mostly conditional loans, leaving it $1.8bn short of its $10bn 2026 target; Norway's up-to-$3bn loan is conditional on reaching $10bn and Canada pledged up to $393m, and one economist warned the fund may not deliver the promised $4 per hectare.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Blended-finance forest vehicles are struggling to reach scale, with payout economics at risk.

themes.theme: Carbon markets, trade and just transition

insights.claim: Technical expert reviews of 16 national Article 6.2 carbon-trading reports found 543 inconsistencies, 115 of them significant, with no report issue-free, yet the COP31 decision merely 'takes note' and does nothing to tighten the 'wild west' rules.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Integrity risk in bilateral carbon-credit trades persists, a reputational and pricing risk for buyers of ITMOs.
insights.locator: Across 16 national reports checked so far

insights.claim: IETA and the Project Developer Forum lobbied that Article 6.4 market rules are too conservative and failing to attract investment; after EU pushback, COP31 only asked the supervisory body to 'take into account' how standards operate together rather than assess their cumulative cost impact, with a rules review due from 2028.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Stringent Paris crediting rules keep project supply and investment slow until at least the 2028 review.
insights.quote: current version of [the market] is failing to attract investment in carbon projects
insights.locator: Andrea Bonzanni, senior director at IETA

insights.claim: Trade measures such as the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) were entirely absent from COP31 outcomes after the cover decision, response-measures and agriculture texts failed, but African states, Kenya and China are expected to push trade harder at COP32.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: CBAM and deforestation rules face growing diplomatic pushback that could escalate at COP32 in Ethiopia.
insights.quote: Unilateral trade measures are only noted. African economies bear their costs
insights.locator: Ghana and Kenya both flagged

insights.claim: COP31 deferred operationalising the new just transition mechanism to COP32 in Ethiopia, but for the first time referenced 'critical minerals' in a COP decision, while removing human-rights due diligence for critical-mineral supply chains.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Critical-mineral supply chains are entering UN climate texts, foreshadowing future ESG/supply-chain expectations.
insights.locator: At COP31, “critical minerals” were referenced

insights.claim: The mitigation work programme, the only COP agenda item dedicated to emissions cuts, was blocked by Saudi Arabia and Russia in the closing plenary, pushing its future to Bonn in 2027; some parties sought to avoid another 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' outcome emerging via the second global stocktake.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Producer states are pre-emptively blocking mechanisms that could produce sectoral targets at COP33.
insights.quote: they want to avoid another sort of transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) situation at COP33
insights.locator: Natalie Jones, senior policy advisor

insights.claim: The Global Carbon Project projects global CO2 emissions of 32.8bn tonnes in 2026, a 0.4% fall versus 2025, driven largely by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions due to the Iran conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while coal emissions continue to rise slightly.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: An oil-supply shock, not policy, is driving the first emissions dip; coal resilience shows the transition remains uneven.
insights.locator: According to the report, CO2 emissions

insights.claim: The WMO reports 2026 will be one of the four warmest years on record, with January–September temperatures about 1.47C above pre-industrial, and an unusually strong 2026-27 El Niño forecast to continue into early 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Heightened physical climate risk into 2027 affects agriculture, insurance and power demand.
insights.quote: this 2026-27 El Niño is off the charts
insights.locator: The report finds that 2026

insights.claim: The UNFCCC's annual NDC synthesis shows emissions falling only around 9% by 2035 versus 2019 if all pledges are implemented, down from a 12% estimate last year, leaving the world substantially off track for 1.5C.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Weakening national pledges imply a slower policy-driven decarbonisation path and higher long-run physical risk.
insights.locator: Based on analysis of the latest NDCs

insights.claim: Methane cuts received a renewed push at COP31 given the 'inevitable' 1.5C overshoot, with $480m in new private funding pledged for methane and other super pollutants and UNEP's alert system flagging leaks in Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico that enabled 125,000 tonnes of methane mitigation.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Methane abatement and monitoring is an investable near-term climate lever with growing funding.
insights.locator: At this event, UNEP announced

insights.claim: China ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028, with a Tsinghua expert attributing the decision to domestic economic pressure on growth and employment; Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand are considering bids, and COP32 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia in November 2027 as the first COP hosted by an LDC.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China is avoiding formal climate leadership while pursuing on-the-ground transition dominance; COP32 will centre finance for developing countries.
insights.locator: During the first week of COP31

insights.claim: The COP31 action agenda grew to 136 'plans to accelerate solutions' and launched voluntary 2035 compacts, including a 25% cut in building energy intensity, at least 15% circular materials in manufacturing, and an 'Antalya AI pledge' on curbing data-centre emissions, alongside a $3m 'climate implementation bridge' with UNDP.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Voluntary compacts flag emerging regulatory attention on data-centre emissions and building efficiency.
